title: Rosalind and the Harvest
premise: Wendell 'Rosalind' Eriksen takes a teaching post in Hollow Creek, where students have been vanishing for decades and the town answers with paperwork and silence. On her first night, the imaginary friend she invented at age seven—Rosalind—is waiting on her porch, unchanged by thirty years, insisting that something taken in 1974 must be returned before the last founding resident, Agnes Voss, signs away the town's deed. As Wendell digs into the school's missing-class problem, she finds Rosalind was never imaginary: she was a girl erased in 1974, and every vanished student since has been a payment to keep the town's prosperity. To save a current missing child and free the trapped, Wendell must expose the covenant outside any court that would hear it, return Rosalind's name to the record, and break the bargain—even though doing so costs the town its fortune and Wendell her carefully constructed invisibility.
about_author: Mirabel Blackwood is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent nine years in towns too small for their own secrets. She writes horror about institutions, ledgers, and the children who fall between them.

chapters.title: The Counted Doors
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. She arrives in Hollow Creek, takes the teaching post, and notices the principal's ritual of counting doors each evening—a habit he calls 'insurance.' The town is prosperous but strangely quiet. Emotional beat: wary curiosity; Wendell, who has always kept herself invisible, feels oddly at home in a place that prefers not to be seen.

chapters.title: Attendance
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Her class roster lists nineteen students; seventeen show up. No one will say where the other two went, and last year's records are sealed in a locked cabinet the janitor won't open. A boy named Theo draws the same face over and over: a girl with no eyes. Emotional beat: unease hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Someone on the Porch
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. At dusk, a woman stands on her porch—exactly as Wendell imagined 'Rosalind' at age seven, down to the crooked braid. Rosalind says only: 'You came back. Now give it back.' Wendell flees inside and finds her childhood drawings, kept by her late mother, all signed with two names. Emotional beat: terror braided with recognition.

chapters.title: What Mother Kept
chapters.summary: POV Wendell, with letters from her mother. The letters reveal Wendell's family lived in Hollow Creek until 1975, then fled overnight. Her mother wrote: 'We took a name with us when we left. Names have weight here.' Emotional beat: grief and betrayal—her invisibility was inherited, engineered.

chapters.title: The Missing-Class Problem
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. She pulls forty years of yearbooks and finds a pattern: every few years one photo is defaced or removed, and the corresponding student simply stops existing in records. Theo's older sister is the most recent. Emotional beat: cold clarity—the vanishings are administrative, deliberate.

chapters.title: Agnes Voss
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. She visits Agnes Voss, ninety-one, the last founding resident, who is preparing to sign the town deed over to a land trust. Agnes is lucid, unafraid, and says: 'The paper keeps it fed. Sign away the paper, starve the thing. Or finish what your grandmother started.' Emotional beat: an offer disguised as a warning.

chapters.title: Rosalind Speaks
chapters.summary: POV alternating Wendell/Rosalind. Rosalind tells her story obliquely through objects: a jump rope, a library card, a shoe. In 1974 she was chosen as the tithe, and Wendell's grandmother, the town clerk, hid Rosalind's true name inside her daughter's imaginary friend—smuggling it out of the ledger. Emotional beat: sorrow becoming kinship; found family forming across death.

chapters.title: The Covenant Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. In the school basement she finds the original 1974 ledger: names traded for harvests, health, and full classrooms. Her grandmother's signature is on the first page—and beside Rosalind's entry, a smudged correction, as if someone tried to strike it. Emotional beat: dread mixed with pride in her grandmother's quiet rebellion.

chapters.title: Theo Disappears
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Theo doesn't come to school. His parents report him 'transferred,' but his bed is unslept-in and his drawings cover the walls—dozens of eyeless girls, now with mouths open, screaming. The principal counts the doors twice that night. Emotional beat: panic; the abstract becomes urgent and personal.

chapters.title: Doors That Count Back
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Wendell realizes the door-counting isn't protection—it's inventory. The building itself is part of the mechanism; certain rooms exist only during the count. She witnesses a hallway stretch where no hallway should be, and hears children humming behind a wall. Emotional beat: vertigo; the school is a mouth.

chapters.title: The Principal's Confession
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Cornered, the principal admits he's a steward, not a villain: his family has kept the count since 1974 because stopping mid-cycle kills everyone owed. He shows her the schedule—Theo is due to be 'collected' at the next new moon, three days after Agnes signs. Emotional beat: moral complexity; loyalty to the town vs. truth.

chapters.title: Loyalty
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Townspeople gently pressure her to drop it: casseroles, kindness, a job offer, then a threat delivered as concern. She understands they aren't evil—they're complicit, and complicity feels like community. For the first time she's tempted to belong. Emotional beat: the seduction of silence.

chapters.title: Truth
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Rosalind forces the choice: 'They love you the way you love a lock—because you keep things in.' Wendell tests them, telling one neighbor the truth outright; by morning her classroom is stripped and her contract voided. Emotional beat: heartbreak and liberation in the same breath.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. There is no court for this—no statute covers trading children for harvests. Wendell assembles her own tribunal: the principal (guilty, useful), the janitor (a witness since 1974), and Agnes. They draft a public reckoning to be read aloud where the ledger was signed. Emotional beat: grim purpose; law fails, so witness must suffice.

chapters.title: The Name in the Record
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Researching county archives, she recovers Rosalind's full name—Rosalind Vane—and learns Agnes was her aunt, who let the tithe happen to protect the family and has signed nothing since out of penance. Returning the name means Agnes admitting it aloud. Emotional beat: mercy and accountability entwined.

chapters.title: New Moon Eve
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Agnes refuses to sign until the reckoning is done; the land-trust lawyers circle; the thing beneath the school grows restless—harvest due, payment short. The humming behind the walls becomes singing. Theo is found standing at the school's locked front door, asleep, waiting to be let in. Emotional beat: countdown dread.

chapters.title: The Reckoning
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. In the basement, before the ledger, Wendell reads the names of every taken child aloud while the principal formally confesses and Agnes speaks Rosalind's name and her own guilt. The ledger begins to burn without fire, entries lifting off the page like ash. Emotional beat: catharsis; testimony as exorcism.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: POV Wendell/Rosalind. The building convulses; the counted doors slam open onto 1974. Wendell walks the old hallway and returns what was taken—not just the name, but the memory, the body's dignity, the story. Rosalind, briefly whole and warm, thanks her and asks to finally be forgotten properly. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness.

chapters.title: Letting Go
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Rosalind fades at dawn, and with her goes the imaginary-friend-shaped hole Wendell had carried since childhood. Theo wakes in his own bed with no memory, but keeps drawing—one girl, eyes open, smiling. Emotional beat: grief that heals instead of hollowing.

chapters.title: The Signature
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. With the covenant broken, Agnes signs the deed freely, dissolving the founding families' claim. The town's unnatural prosperity falters—crops thin, budgets tighten—but people stay, some for the first time choosing the place honestly. The principal burns the door-count book. Emotional beat: sober hope; justice costs.

chapters.title: Harvest
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Autumn comes ordinary and plain. Wendell stays on as teacher, no longer invisible—her students know her, argue with her, need her. At the harvest festival she sets a place at the table for Rosalind Vane, and the town, unprompted, adds nineteen more plates. Emotional beat: belonging earned through truth.

chapters.title: Porch Light
chapters.summary: POV Wendell, epilogue. Years later, a new teacher arrives in Hollow Creek and Wendell gives her the honest version of the town's history. That night, on Wendell's porch, nothing waits—only the porch light she leaves burning anyway, for anyone still finding their way home. Final beat: peace without forgetting; the vigil continues by choice.
